In [[mathematics]], in the realm of [[group theory]], an '''IA automorphism''' of a [[group (mathematics)|group]] is an [[automorphism]] that acts as identity on the [[abelianization]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Bachmuth | first = S.
 | journal = Transactions of the American Mathematical Society
 | mr = 0190212
 | pages = 1–17
 | title = Induced automorphisms of free groups and free metabelian groups
 | volume = 122
 | year = 1966
 | doi=10.2307/1994498| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> The abelianization of a group is its [[quotient group|quotient]] by its [[commutator subgroup]]. An IA automorphism is thus an automorphism that sends each [[coset]] of the commutator subgroup to itself.

The IA automorphisms of a group form a [[normal subgroup]] of the automorphism group. Every [[inner automorphism]] is an IA automorphism, since inner automorphisms act trivially on the abelianization and the group of inner automorphisms is normal in the full automorphism group of any group.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Inner automorphisms form a normal subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/824062/inner-automorphisms-form-a-normal-subgroup-of-operatornameautg |access-date=2026-01-26 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange |language=en}}</ref>

For free groups, the study of IA automorphisms is important in understanding the structure of the automorphism group and its subgroups, as these automorphisms often preserve significant algebraic properties of the group.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Combinatorial Group Theory: Presentations of Groups in Terms of Generators and Relations {{!}} Mathematical Association of America |url=https://old.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/combinatorial-group-theory-presentations-of-groups-in-terms-of-generators-and-relations |access-date=2026-01-06 |website=old.maa.org}}</ref> These automorphisms are particularly studied in relation to the lower central series and the behavior of commutator subgroups, providing insight into the intrinsic symmetries of free groups.
